summary: This memo is an updated policy statement on the schedule for implementing the Domain Style Naming System. It updates RFC 881 and RFC 897 and is an official statement of the IAB and DARPA, pointing elsewhere for how the system itself works.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 921 revises the plan for moving Internet hosts from flat names and a central host table to hierarchical domain names and distributed name servers. It lists milestones for the transition and explains that names and lookup methods change in separate steps.

subtitle: The revised schedule for moving Internet hosts to hierarchical domain names.

tldr.problem: The earlier plans for adopting domain-style names and name servers had not been completed on schedule. Hosts still relied on simple names and a centrally maintained host table.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB and DARPA policy memo separates the changes to naming from the changes to name lookup, then sets revised dates for establishing the domain table, registering domains, using resolvers, and retiring the complete host table.
tldr.outcome: RFC 921 updates RFC 881 and RFC 897. It is a schedule and policy statement, while RFC 882 and RFC 883 describe how the name service works.

today: RFC 921 updates RFC 881 and RFC 897. Its schedule is from 1984 and 1985; it points to RFC 882 and RFC 883 for the system design.

sections.title: From Flat Names to Domain Names
sections.content:
The memo describes a change from simple host names to structured names made of components separated by periods. The components are written from the most specific on the left to the most general on the right. At the time, the new names generally appended .ARPA to an earlier simple name.

Name lookup also relied on a centrally maintained table called HOSTS.TXT, which hosts copied from the Network Information Center. The memo describes a future system in which multiple servers each hold part of the name-to-address information.
sections.plainLanguage: Names are changing from one flat list of host names to names with a hierarchy of parts. Lookup is also planned to move from one central table to distributed servers.

sections.title: The Planned Name-Service Transition
sections.content:
The memo describes several stages in the use of domain names. First, domain-style names replace old host names while still being looked up in the central table. Later, names can contain more components and can refer to organizations as well as individual hosts. In that case, a name server can identify a host that handles mail for an organization.

The transition consists of two separate changes: adopting domain-style names, then replacing central-table lookup with name servers. The DARPA research community is expected to make both changes. The DDN operational community follows the naming schedule but is not required to move to name servers at the same time.
sections.plainLanguage: The transition changes the names first and the lookup system second. The memo gives the DARPA and DDN communities different requirements for the second change.

sections.title: Managing Host Renames
sections.content:
The memo expects every host to change its name at least once, and some hosts may change names several times as they move into new domains. Renaming can disrupt replies to old mail, copied addresses, and mailing-list entries.

One transition measure is to keep an old name as a nickname for a period, so that systems can still find the host. The distributed database must preserve the ability to look up a host from any of its names and to find its primary name from its address.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing a host's name can make old addresses stop working. Keeping the old name as a nickname for a while helps systems reach the host during the transition.

sections.title: The Revised Implementation Dates
sections.content:
The schedule has three broad parts: putting servers and resolvers in place, installing the database, and updating user programs such as mailers. The memo says that the protocol and database specifications had been published and that servers for the ARPA domain were operating, while little work had yet been done on user programs.

The listed milestones run from a top-level domain table at the NIC on 15 December 1984 to a possible DDN plan on 15 October 1985. Between them, the schedule calls for domain registration to begin on 15 January, major machinery to be ready on 15 February, applications to begin regular use in May, and the naming-system transition to be complete in July. The NIC host table need no longer be complete for the DARPA research community by 15 September.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo sets dates for building the lookup system, opening domain registration, updating programs, and reducing reliance on the central host table. It also records which tasks from the earlier schedule had not been completed.

events.label: 15 Dec: top-level domain table at the NIC
15 May: regular use of resolvers and servers begins
15 Jul: domain naming system transition completed
15 Sep: NIC host table need not be complete for DARPA research hosts
15 Oct: possible DDN plan for name service
